name: quest-ai-runner library
description: A domain-free Python library: a bounded plan, gather, re-plan, answer loop that escalates to a deep runner when real work is needed (the core), a task executor that polls Quest, claims, runs, escalates and reports (the runner), and reference adapters for retrieval, model providers, cards, vectors, web research and deep runners, all wired by one configuration per lane and each swappable part chosen by metric.
advantages: One engine for chat and scheduled work; grounded in the consumer's sources; escalation built in; open source and reusable outside Quest; every part measured and swappable.
disadvantages: A large codebase to maintain; chat answer quality is currently weak on the cheapest model; some parts are measured only offline; consumers must keep adapters in step with the library.

name: Per-consumer worker
description: Each product writes its own worker and chat backend around a model vendor's API.
advantages: Fits its one product exactly; no shared-library coordination.
disadvantages: The plumbing is rebuilt and drifts per product (the history that led to QAR); improvements do not travel; chat and tasks diverge.

name: Agent framework with Quest glue
description: Build the engine from a general framework (LangGraph, CrewAI, an agent SDK) and add Quest grounding, escalation and the executor as glue.
advantages: Mature building blocks, community and tooling; less code of our own for the loop.
disadvantages: Grounding, scope containment, escalation, the executor and measured selection still have to be built; framework churn becomes a dependency risk.

name: Deep runner only
description: Hand every task straight to a coding agent such as Claude Code with the person's material available, with no routing or answering loop in front.
advantages: Strong at real multi-step work; very little engine code.
disadvantages: Slow and costly for simple questions; weaker grounding in Quest's own state; escalation and scope still need building; one vendor dependency.

name: Keyless command-line provider
description: Drives the local Claude command-line tool in print mode so planning and answering run on the operator's subscription login. Planning asks for only the decision JSON and parses leniently, and the spawned process has API credentials stripped from its environment.
advantages: No API key and no per-token billing, so a whole runner can operate on a subscription alone.
disadvantages: Spawning a process adds latency, the tool cannot force a tool choice, and tiers are limited to the model families the tool can run.

name: Prefix-routing multi-provider
description: Wraps a primary provider and a set of vendor providers, routes each call by model-name prefix, steps down a tier when a quota error occurs, and applies shared retry for transient errors. Callers see one provider.
advantages: Vendor and tier changes are configuration, and quota exhaustion degrades service instead of failing. It beats a single flat provider on the offline cases. Selected because: QAR_MODEL_BACKEND and ModelRegistry tiers
disadvantages: More moving parts and a per-call routing decision. Fallback hides a degraded tier unless logged, and price knowledge is input-only.

name: Single flat provider floor
description: A baseline in which every model name goes to one provider, a quota error is final, transient errors are not retried, the dry run counts input only and every model has the same price. It is the floor the multi-provider stack must beat.
advantages: Trivially simple and predictable, and it shows the value of each added capability by removal.
disadvantages: No resilience, no tier-aware cost, and one vendor outage stops everything.

name: MCP gateway bridge transport
description: Wraps a generic MCP client to speak a small fixed set of gateway tools: long-poll for events to receive, send a message, and best-effort attachment fetch. It deliberately has no code path that responds to the gateway's own permission requests, clamps the poll timeout and tolerates key spelling drift.
advantages: Reuses a maintained gateway so many chat networks become channels without new code, and its small tool surface limits risk. Selected because: RunnerConfig.channel_transport
disadvantages: Depends on the gateway's availability and security posture and on guessed payload shapes. Only one channel family is covered.

name: Fake-gateway conformance arm
description: Drives the production channel with a fake MCP client injected at the process edge and records ids, texts, health, poll timeout, attachment sizes and whether only allowed tools were called.
advantages: Offline, fast and deterministic, with the real production class under test.
disadvantages: Proves agreement with the assumed wire shapes, not with a real gateway, until a recorded fixture exists.

name: Digest-driven overseer
description: Builds a capped compact digest of the run, makes one structured model call with a fixed prompt and tool schema, validates the answer against the five signals, and returns proceed on any error, non-object response or unknown signal.
advantages: Very low token cost, safe by default, and cannot distort a run without an explicit signal. Selected because: RunnerConfig.overseer
disadvantages: Quality rests on the digest keeping the right evidence and on a model deciding well, and the live signal match is unmeasured.

name: No-judgement digest probe
description: A floor arm that always returns no signal, so the scorer measures only whether the digest shows the evidence each label turns on.
advantages: Free, offline and isolates the digest from model judgment.
disadvantages: Says nothing about whether the model reads the evidence correctly.

name: Live overseer model arm
description: Calls the production overseer function against the real provider, one small call per scenario, and fails if the overseer degraded.
advantages: Measures actual signal correctness with the production prompt.
disadvantages: Needs a model backend and spend, and has not been recorded.

name: Task poller and claimer
description: Discovers due tasks per scan, deduplicates by signature across restarts, claims through the backend, hands each task to the executor with bounded concurrency, and pauses pickup when the host is overloaded.
advantages: Event-driven, restart-safe, and degrades instead of crashing on transient errors.
disadvantages: Large and stateful, with several guards that interact, so edge cases such as orphaned claims are hard to see.

name: Single-task executor
description: Runs one claimed task through the orchestrator and maps the result onto a status report: answer or met deep run is done, a short deep run is incomplete or failed, a decision is needs-you, a cancelled task gets no report. It never raises to the poller.
advantages: One clear unit of work that is easy to test with a mock client and stub brain.
disadvantages: The mapping from result to status is policy that must stay in step with the backend's status vocabulary.

name: Configured persona resolver
description: Chooses who runs a task from configuration, in order: a structured assignment field matching the registry, an optional model-judged explicit ask, then domain dominance, with optional auto-registration of unknown ids.
advantages: Replaces hand-written resolvers, needs no model call for structural lanes, and never activates on a bare name mention.
disadvantages: The judged and dominance steps depend on model judgement, and a wrong registry entry misroutes work.

name: Work-folder sync
description: Mirrors a work item's state and notes into a local file with runner-managed marked sections, and pushes new human notes back once, preserving human-authored text elsewhere in the file.
advantages: Idempotent, keeps human edits, and uses only the existing client methods.
disadvantages: A single shared file can conflict with hand edits near the markers, and direction rules must be respected by callers.

name: Shared lane entry point
description: Provides the check, once and loop-forever driver with argument parsing, env-file loading, local-time due gating and degrade-instead-of-crash behaviour on incomplete config.
advantages: Removes the duplicated glue each consumer used to write.
disadvantages: Consumers must fit its argv shape, and the local-time gate patches behaviour globally.

name: Offline lifecycle harness
description: Runs the real poller, executor, persona resolver, folder sync, scheduling helper and lane helpers against a fake client and a scripted model, with no model calls.
advantages: Deterministic and free coverage of the whole lifecycle including duplicates, lost claims and team scoping. Selected because: runner/config_wiring.py (a lane's run_lane drives Poller and TaskExecutor)
disadvantages: The fake client hides wire-level behaviour such as HTTP errors and real payload shapes, and crash recovery of orphaned claims is not yet covered.

name: Static price table lookup
description: Holds a snapshot of list prices per million input tokens by provider and model, detects the provider from the environment, falls back to a stated default for unknown models, and estimates bootstrap cost from a token count.
advantages: Simple, offline and instant, and gives a cost estimate before any spend.
disadvantages: Hand-maintained, input tokens only, and stale until someone edits it.

name: Persisted daily token tracker
description: Counts input and output tokens within a UTC day, persists the tally to a JSON file so a restart reloads it, resets at the day boundary, and reports over-limit and a status line. A limit of zero or off disables it.
advantages: Survives restarts and cleanly separates days; opt-in so it never surprises a lane.
disadvantages: Counts tokens, not money, and a deep runner on a subscription is outside the count; a lost usage file resets the day.

name: Hysteresis resource guard
description: Samples memory use, free memory and load, pauses new work when a limit is exceeded and resumes only after readings clear, and can wait until the host is fine. Sampling uses the process file system or a library, with limits from code or the environment.
advantages: Hysteresis prevents flapping, and pausing is lossless because unclaimed work stays queued.
disadvantages: Thresholds are manual and host-specific, and the sampler depends on platform facilities that may be absent.

name: Live usage evaluation arm
description: Drives the live price, estimate, tracker and guard code, with a real usage file in a scratch folder and scripted host samples as the only fake.
advantages: Verifies arithmetic and persistence against real code with no model calls. Selected because: runner/poller.py (ResourceGuard, DailyUsageTracker) and cli_context bootstrap estimate
disadvantages: Cannot notice that real prices have changed, only that the table is internally right.

name: Apply the evolvable-structure library
description: QAR keeps its specifications as records under esoi and builds on the library's solutions to apply a project's structure: the application procedure, the structure check, the measurement harness and the implementation selector.
advantages: No checker of QAR's own to maintain; every part is compared on the same cases and selected by its metric. Selected because: the evolvable-structure library already carries the machinery; QAR keeps only its records and configuration
disadvantages: A dependency pinned by commit, and a runtime one because implementations are declared with its decorators; a rule or format change in the library needs a migration here; offline arms only unless a paid arm is run by decision.

name: Rebuilt prompt per step with a referenced context (today)
description: Each step is a fresh planner call built from the template, the cached head and context layers, the newest observations in full and older ones in one line; from the second step the transcript and the context block are replaced by a short note that refers to step one.
advantages: Built and selected; the smallest planner input per step; the final answer still sees everything.
disadvantages: From the second step the planner sees neither the transcript nor the context block, and is told it saw them; continuity across steps is unmeasured.

name: Rebuilt prompt per step with the context re-sent from cache
description: The same per-step call with the reference note switched off (planner_abbreviate_repeat_context), so every step re-sends the transcript and context block as an unchanged prefix a caching provider reads from cache.
advantages: No new code; every step sees what the first saw; the cached prefix stays identical across steps.
disadvantages: Pays for the context on every step, cheaply only where the provider caches it, which is unmeasured here; a step still sees earlier steps only through their observations.

name: Carried message stream per request (proposed)
description: Proposed. One message list per request: the first step's prompt opens it, each step adds its decision and the observations admitted to it, and the provider's prefix cache covers everything before the newest step, as a coding agent's session does.
advantages: Closest to the session that makes a coding agent reliable; each step sees every earlier step's reasoning; cache reads keep the repeat cost low.
disadvantages: Grows with every step; a wrong item stays for the rest of the request; needs a many-message plan call on every provider, including those that render the tool schema into the prompt; not built.

name: Carried stream with compaction (proposed)
description: Proposed. The carried stream, compacted to a summary of its settled part when it passes a budget, keeping refusals, corrections and the resolved request word for word.
advantages: Bounded cost on long requests while keeping a stream's continuity.
disadvantages: Each compaction can drop a detail a later step needs and costs a model call; the compaction rule is one more thing to measure; not built.

name: Start-of-run card filter and a recency window (today)
description: Cards are filtered once from the request text at the start of the run; afterwards every observation is admitted, the newest few in full and older ones in one line.
advantages: Built; no model call per step; a short run sees everything it read.
disadvantages: Blind to the goal: a finding that matters can be collapsed and a near miss is admitted like a match; the scope fence is applied per store rather than at one gate.

name: Small-model judge of every candidate (proposed)
description: Proposed. Every candidate item is judged by a small model against the goal condition before it is admitted.
advantages: Understands relevance and near misses; gives a reason per item.
disadvantages: At least one model call per step and its latency on the fast path; not built.

name: Score thresholds per source (proposed)
description: Proposed. Retrieval scores and the item's source decide admission with fixed thresholds, with no model call.
advantages: Free, fast and deterministic.
disadvantages: Scores do not know the goal, so near misses with high word overlap get through; not built.

name: Thresholds with a judge on the borderline (proposed)
description: Proposed. Thresholds settle clear admits and clear drops; only items in a borderline band go to a small model asked whether the item bears on the goal.
advantages: Likely the cheapest accurate mix: most steps make no model call.
disadvantages: Two stages and a band to tune; not built.

name: Web research with the answer's support check (today)
description: World questions are answered from the model's knowledge and snippet-first web research, and the answer check flags claims the turn's reads do not support and rewrites them once with their basis.
advantages: Built; cheap and fast; unsupported claims are hedged rather than asserted.
disadvantages: No evidence-strength label; a host's research sources are not consulted unless wired as a retrieval source or a tool; general knowledge that passes the check is still stated without a source.

name: Host research sources first, then the web (proposed)
description: Proposed. A host declares its research and experience search interfaces; a world question goes to them first and to the web only when they do not cover it, and each finding carries its source and an evidence label.
advantages: Uses the strongest evidence the host has; one shape of finding whatever the source; the web stays the fallback.
disadvantages: Each host must declare and maintain its sources; research interfaces are slower than snippets; not built.

name: Findings weighed by a host's evidence-estimation service (proposed)
description: Proposed. As research_sources_first, with each finding passed to a host's evidence-estimation service that returns how strongly the evidence supports it, stated with the answer.
advantages: Calibrated confidence the person can weigh; the same estimate everywhere the product answers.
disadvantages: Depends on a host service and its cost and latency; not every question has an estimate; the specification owner does not plan to bring such evidence operations into this chat (2026-10-28), so it is recorded as an alternative only; not built.

name: Managed quest card plus optional live reads (today)
description: A managed card per quest, rebuilt when the quest syncs, grounds each turn, and the planner issues live reads through the host's retrieval adapter when it wants more.
advantages: Built; cheap; one card per quest that every surface shares.
disadvantages: The card lags changes made since the last sync, including the AI's own; reads are optional; nothing is read back after a change, so two answers in a session can rest on different reads.

name: Read back what a change touched (proposed)
description: Proposed. After every operation the objects it touched are re-read and placed in the working stream, replacing older views of them for the rest of the session.
advantages: The AI's own changes never contradict what it says next; one small read per change.
disadvantages: Changes made by others still lag until the next read; not built.

name: A live read behind every state claim (proposed)
description: Proposed. Every claim about account state needs a live read in the same turn; no card is used for state.
advantages: Always current, including others' changes.
disadvantages: A read on every state question costs time on the reply path; not built.

name: Separate stores read at the start of a request (today)
description: Conversation recall, recent context, feedback guidance, predictions, reflections and quest cards are each read separately at the start of a request and prepended to the context block, fenced per quest or global; a representative's learned notes and context preferences are read with no scope; declined proposals arrive from the host's escalation history.
advantages: Built; each store is measured on its own; a failure in one does not stop the others.
disadvantages: No view of what an intent or the quest settled; several budgets and paths, each of which must apply the fence; the representative's notes cross quests; chat and background work read different subsets.

name: Maintained view per quest only (proposed)
description: Proposed. After each request a cheap model rewrites, in the background, a short note for the quest of what was decided, declined, learned and is next, each line citing its source; every request on that quest reads it first. This is the lowest level of the hierarchy, with nothing above it.
advantages: Simple; the fence stays the existing per-quest tag; no time added before the reply.
disadvantages: Nothing learned at an intent above the quest reaches it, which is the gap the owner named; a wrong line persists until corrected; not built.

name: Periodic reflection on the best tier (proposed)
description: Proposed. On a schedule a best-tier model reviews a quest's recent requests and outcomes and writes its long view.
advantages: A true long view from few calls.
disadvantages: Stale between runs; best-tier cost; not built.

name: Intuition: outcome precedents surfaced at admission (proposed)
description: Proposed. Each finished request is logged by the long view with its kind and how it ended (accepted, refused, stuck, contradicted); at admission a new request is matched to similar past ones without a model call, and a precedent that ended badly is admitted to the working stream as a hint, never as a decision.
advantages: Model-free and cheap; turns the history of failures into a warning before the same step repeats.
disadvantages: Word similarity misses paraphrase; outcome labels need a signal from the host (a refusal, a rework); overlaps recipe replay for operations that succeeded; a hint the planner ignores changes nothing; not built.

name: No overseer (configuration off)
description: The overseer switched off, so a run is exactly what the planner and its own checks do, with no watcher and no overseer call.
advantages: No cost or latency; nothing argues with a correct decision.
disadvantages: Nothing catches drift, wasted reads or a needed hand-off in a run nobody watches; never compared with the overseer on the same runs.

name: Overseer that asks questions of fact (proposed)
description: Proposed. Instead of judging the run, the overseer asks one or two narrow questions of fact from the digest (has the goal condition been met by what was gathered; is the pending proposal one the person declined; is what is still needed within reach), and the answers reach the working stream as facts while the planner keeps the decision.
advantages: Follows the measured pattern where a question of fact beat a review of the decision; the stronger tier still reads few tokens.
disadvantages: A fact the planner ignores changes nothing; fixed questions can miss a new kind of failure; not built.

name: Code-enforced before and after on deep runs only (today)
description: Around every deep goal the slice is found, the metric is read before and after by the runner's meters, rows go to the ledger, and a changed run with nothing on record is asked once and otherwise marked missing; chat turns and in-process work are not covered.
advantages: Built and shown in the terminal and the host's chat; decided from the ledger, never from words.
disadvantages: Covers only deep runs; nothing acts on a regression or a missing metric; no metric is proposed when none applies.

name: Standing instruction alone (floor)
description: The standing instructions ask the AI to say what the relevant metric was before and after; nothing in code reads, records or checks it.
advantages: No cost or latency; works wherever a prompt reaches.
disadvantages: Depends on the model's wording and memory, which is what the owner ruled out; kept only as the floor that shows what code enforcement adds.

name: Every request measured by code (proposed)
description: Proposed. Chat turns and in-process work pass the same begin and finish as a deep goal: the slice, or the quest's own specification, is found at the start; the reading before comes from the cheap recorded-row meter; the reading after is taken in the background after the reply; the row is written to the ledger and shown in the explanation of how the answer was reached.
advantages: One rule for chat, tasks and deep work; the reply does not wait; reuses the existing modules.
disadvantages: Most chat turns change nothing a metric can see, so many readings are empty; a background reading arrives after the person has moved on; not built.

name: Measured, proposed and answered (proposed)
description: Proposed. As every_request_measured, plus: a request with no slice or no metric gets a metric proposed to the owner, never a reading invented; a reading that got worse gets one bounded response in the same run (a retry or a revert), else a follow-up task on the record with the reading, else an escalation only when a person must choose; a missing metric becomes a follow-up. For a person's quest, an uncertain choice becomes a proposed experiment.
advantages: Closes the loop: no regression or missing metric is only displayed; the records grow where they are thin.
disadvantages: Proposals and follow-ups add work for the owner if they are many; a revert must never undo what the person asked for; an experiment needs the person's consent; not built.

name: Per-risk response chosen by metric (proposed)
description: Proposed. A registry of risk categories, each with a cheap detector over the run's own records and a response chosen by that category's metric (a stronger tier, one narrow question of fact, a rule, a hand-off to deep work or a person); a response is kept only while it beats no response on its category with statistical significance.
advantages: Spends review only where risk is; each risk gets what works for it; a response that does not help is dropped by measurement, not taste.
disadvantages: Needs a detector and a labelled case set per category, and rare risks need many cases to reach significance; more parts to keep; not built.

name: One view per intent, cascading down (proposed)
description: Proposed. One maintained view per intent, shared by any representative serving it; a request reads the view of its quest's intent and of each ancestor, nearest first, within a budget, fenced so a view reaches only its intent's descendants.
advantages: Follows the host's hierarchy directly; one view per intent whoever serves it; reuses the placements and parent links the host already stores.
disadvantages: Representatives with different roles share one view and blur it; deep chains cost tokens; needs a fence that knows ancestors; not built.

name: One view per representative across its assigned quests, placed in the hierarchy (proposed, recommended)
description: Proposed. Each AI representative keeps one maintained high-level view across the quests assigned to it (decisions, declines, corrections, learned notes, where the work is heading), anchored at the lowest intent that holds those quests and reading that intent's ancestors within a budget. A request it handles reads that view and the parts of its single quest's detail that bear on it. Its existing learned notes and context preferences are filed under the quest or intent they were learned in, so they gain the same fence.
advantages: Matches the owner's model: the representative and its assigned quests are the unit, with a broad view across them; reuses the host's quest assignments, roles and intent placements; gives the representative's notes the scope they lack today.
disadvantages: A representative's quests may sit under several intents, so the anchor can be wide; the view must be rebuilt when an assignment changes; notes learned before this have no quest or intent and must be placed or kept global; needs the fence that knows assignments and ancestors; not built.

name: Registered prompt specs with an enforcement test (today)
description: Prompts are declared as PromptSpecs and a test with a shrinking baseline lists the call sites that are not yet registered.
advantages: Built; every registered prompt carries its owner solution, metric and no-em-dash rule.
disadvantages: Not measured; some call sites are still unregistered (the enforcement baseline lists them), there is no ablation, and spend-weighted value is not computed.

name: Registry plus per-call ablation against the owner metric (proposed)
description: Proposed. Each call is dropped or downgraded in turn and the owner metric is read again on production-shaped cases; budgets are set from the value shown.
advantages: Shows what each call earns and finds cheaper or faster options.
disadvantages: Paid runs per prompt, and only as good as each owner metric; not built.

name: Registry read together with the code (today)
description: Reads the hub registry and the code: declared implementations, solution records, a static scan of core for vendor branches, and a fake hub registered through each area configuration entry.
advantages: Free, offline and deterministic; a new area is data; shows which areas still need code per integration.
disadvantages: Findings come from web search by hand, so research freshness is only as honest as the dates recorded; six areas have no fake-hub probe yet.

name: Channels, terminal and package as ways in
description: Each way in is its own measured solution, and every one hands its request to the same router. The package's front door is taught by its documents (explain-qar), shown by its examples (learn-by-example) and set up through one layered configuration (configure-a-lane).
advantages: A new channel is one more solution beneath this one, measured on its own.
disadvantages: No metric judges the ways in together; only each one's own.

name: Quest HTTP client from the environment
description: Builds the Quest client from QUEST_BASE_URL (or QUEST_API_URL), QUEST_API_KEY and, when set, QUEST_TEAM_ID, so the runner works in the account those name.
advantages: One client for every consumer of the runner; nothing to pass when the environment is set.
disadvantages: Reads one account; a deployment that serves several teams passes its own client.
